title: Action and capability registries wrapping the existing pipeline steps
description: Second runtime child of 209. The registry of named actions - each wrapping an existing trusted pipeline step (claim, develop, publish, check, review, promote, clean up) - with the capabilities each requires declared in code. Configuration will choose sequence from these names; it can never mint one, which is the epic's capability-stays-trusted-code law. No caller changes: the existing hard-coded pipeline keeps calling its steps directly; the registry is a second door onto the same functions. Done means: every step the delivery pipeline executes today has a registered action naming its capability requirements; the registry refuses duplicate names and unknown capabilities at construction, tested; a repository test asserts the registry's coverage against the pipeline's actual step set so a later step cannot be added unregistered silently; existing behavior is byte-for-byte unchanged (the 211 golden traces still pass unmodified); the diff is shown whole to review. Dispatch waits on the hardening freeze.

title: Workflow definition schema: versioned, digest-pinned, validated
description: First runtime child of the configurable-workflows epic (209), per the landed design's conversion order. The declarative workflow-definition format: versioned schema for states, transitions, and action references; a content digest computed over the definition so instances can pin to it; validation types that make an ill-formed definition unrepresentable rather than checked later. No execution, no loader wiring, no behavior change - existing pipeline code untouched. Done means: the schema exists as Go types with a stable serialized form; the digest is deterministic and tested against fixture definitions; validation rejects unknown fields, dangling transition targets, and actions naming no registered capability, each with a test; nothing in the existing delivery path imports or depends on any of it yet; the diff is shown whole to review. Dispatch waits on the hardening freeze per the epic's note.

title: The four-line status: running, working, not-startable-with-reasons, needs-a-human
description:
Operator directive, 2026-08-30, admitted at the queue front - his third ask for clear running-state in two days, with each stall's confusion tracing to its absence. The rendering surface for the certainty contract (139), in the ratified four-line format whose quoted example is the canonical fixture:

Running (N developer runs) - each with item, phase, elapsed, spend.
Working (N conversations) - the persona turns in flight, which no surface counts today.
Not startable - each ready-but-unstarted item with its named reason taken from the real refusal, never session memory.
Needs a human - always present: 'nothing' or the explicit list with whose-move.

A state that cannot render into these four lines is a bug in the state. Lands first on the CLI (yoyo status or the builder's naming) per the contract's CLI-first sequencing, serving from the read model's query where it exists and from the truest available sources meanwhile - the format must not wait for 139's full machinery to say what is already knowable, but must converge on the one query as it lands. The heartbeat adopts the same four lines. Done means the operator's example renders from live state, all four lines always print, the working line counts conversation turns for the first time, and no residual category exists anywhere in the output.

The acceptance clauses are met and tested: all four lines always render (TestQuietHarnessPrintsAllFourLines pins the exact text), the operator's quoted example renders from live state (TestTheOperatorsExampleRendersFromState), the working line counts conversation turns from the lease for the first time (TestWorkingCountsOnlyHeldConversations), and the absence of a residual bucket is asserted at the CLI level. The unreadable-versus-empty discipline is held consistently — an unreadable source, an unreadable switch, an unwired source, and an unpriceable run each have a test proving they are never reported as nothing or as free — and the heartbeat states the absence of the lines rather than omitting them. No delivered invariant is violated: nothing here writes to the repository, invokes a role, touches a promotion lease, claims work, or stores durable state in a provider session. docs/operations.md and docs/reporting.md were updated alongside, and I found no document in the patch left asserting something the change made false, beyond the one example-line discrepancy below. All four checks pass and they exercise the new behaviour rather than merely compiling it. The observations below are minor and do not block.
Finding [minor] (docs/operations.md:600): The documented canonical example cannot be produced by the renderer. readNeedsHuman formats attention as `fmt.Sprintf("directive %s is unresolved: %s", paused.ID, ...)`, which yields `directive <ID> is unresolved`, but the example line reads `directive-4f2c… is unresolved` with a hyphen and no space. Either the example has a typo, or directive IDs carry a `directive-` prefix (as run-… and chat-… IDs here do) and the rendered line stutters as `directive directive-4f2c… is unresolved`. Reconcile the two, and check `run %s of %s ended still owing a step` for the same stutter against `run-…` IDs.
Finding [minor] (internal/readmodel/standing.go:330): readWorking answers "is a turn in flight" by acquiring and immediately releasing each recorded conversation's exclusive advisory lease. That probe previously ran only under `yoyo agent`, an explicit inspection verb; it now runs on every `yoyo status` and on the Slack heartbeat, which is a long-lived background process. A conversation that tries to start inside the probe's window sees ErrConversationHeld and may report itself as somebody else's conversation. The window is tiny, but consider whether a shared/read probe or a retry on the acquiring side is warranted now that a background process takes these locks periodically.
Finding [minor] (internal/cli/status.go:270): standingSources silently drops the error from every store constructor except the tracker, leaving the source nil, so the line then reports "nothing was wired to read …" when what actually happened is that the state directory would not open. The comment on unreadableTracker states the right rule — "so the line says what actually went wrong instead of reporting a wiring gap" — and applies it only to the tracker. Carrying the construction error the same way for the run, conversation, hold, and session stores would make the four lines say the real cause to an operator debugging a broken state root.
Finding [minor] (internal/cli/status.go:162): The item's done clause reads "all four lines always print", and the change omits them entirely when an item is named. The rationale is coherent and is documented in operations.md, the usage text, and a test, so I am not treating it as incomplete — but it is a product decision beyond the literal clause and the operator may want it confirmed, since `yoyo status <id>` is a common invocation that now answers a strictly narrower question than the directive described.

Review decision: approve
Review summary: The change delivers the operator-DM tier as the item scopes it and reconciles it cleanly with the steer machinery on current main. Outbound: the ask is derived in HarnessFeed.heartbeatDeliveries beside the channel line it already computes, so the channel and the DM cannot disagree about what stopped the line or what would unstop it; it is carried on Batch.Asking and put to each operator separately as a brief top line plus a threaded, numbered context, once per state per person via the new DecisionMap, and a refused conversations.open costs one message rather than the pass. Inbound: readInbound now carries the conversation instead of filtering on it, and handle routes on the sink's own channel id, so a channel thread still steers its work item (covered by a regression test) and a DM thread the sink asked in is decided; a DM thread the sink did not open is correctly left alone. The three tests the prior refusal named are present and would fail without the change — parseDecision's grammar and its refusal of a number naming no option, decide's authority-first check and the recorded directive, and the full reply-in-thread-is-the-decision path through steering.handle. Invariant checks: the reply records one unscoped operational directive through the existing directive store and nothing is carried out, so surfaces-project-one-read-model's directive path holds and no second invoker is introduced; decisions.json goes through Store.write under the same declared root as the thread, cursor and steer maps; nothing here makes a provider session the only copy of anything. Documentation in docs/reporting.md, docs/slack/setup.md, docs/slack/manifest.yaml and the CLI help matches the implemented top line, threaded ask, scope-manifest pairing and failure lines I could check against the code. Two minor observations follow; neither blocks.
Finding [minor] (internal/slack/inbound.go:471): A reply typed at the top level of the DM rather than in the ask's thread is dropped with no answer at all: readInbound still requires a thread_ts, and handle never reaches decideThread for it. That is the likeliest reply on the surface the top line was designed for — a phone notification opens the flat DM conversation, not the thread — and silence there is the one outcome this package elsewhere says an operator must never get. If the threaded-only correlation is to stand as designed, consider at least answering an un-threaded DM message that arrives in a conversation the decision map knows, telling the person to reply in the thread, so a decision they believe they made is not lost quietly.
Finding [minor] (internal/slack/state.go:360): DecisionMap grows monotonically and is never pruned: every mark is timestamped, so each distinct stopped state ever asked about keeps one entry per operator forever, and AskedOf scans all of them each pass. If it ever reaches maxRecordBytes, LoadDecisions fails and both halves stop — nobody is asked and no reply is read. Dropping entries whose mark is no longer the standing state would bound it.

One minor observation follows; it does not block.
Finding [minor] (internal/slack/decision.go:160): DecisionMap.Latest picks the most recent remembered ask in a conversation with no bound on how old it is or whether its state still stands, so once an operator has been asked anything, every top-level message they ever type in that DM is answered with "Nothing was recorded" pointing at that ask — which may name a state that cleared weeks earlier and a thread that is about to be forgotten. Consider not answering when the remembered ask is no longer the standing state, or saying that the ask it names has since cleared, so the pointer never sends somebody to a thread about a line that is already moving.

title: Worktree cleanup keeps the sandbox viable: prune stale registrations, bound the deny list
description: Critical report from the developer on 82.2's run, 2026-08-23: every Bash command in that worktree fails at spawn with E2BIG - the sandbox profile adds 335 filesystem deny paths per command, 168 of them for registered git worktrees, and the list grows without bound as the harness creates worktrees. That run was documentation-only and cost nothing; the next code change in that environment cannot run make check, go test, or bd at all. Immediate remedy per the report: git worktree prune and stale-worktree removal on the machine. The durable fix: the harness cleans up its per-item worktrees - many run records this month carry 'worktree (cleanup pending)' - so registrations do not accumulate into the deny list until command spawning breaks. Done means the machine's registered-worktree count reflects live runs plus a bounded tail, cleanup runs as part of settle or reconcile rather than by hand, and a command in a fresh worktree spawns with a deny list that does not scale with harness history.

Reason: Isolation machinery whose accumulated residue makes verification impossible is the worktree goal consuming itself; on the affected machine every future code run fails at spawn, which is a stall in progress, not a risk. Priority 1 at the frontier.

title: The release gate commits the tracker's derived exports instead of refusing on them
description:
Operator-directed from v0.3.0's first cut, 2026-08-23, deadline: before the product manager's first delegated release tomorrow. The cut refused because .beads/interactions.jsonl and .beads/issues.jsonl were dirty - derived exports that mutate whenever anything touches the tracker, including the walkthrough the gate itself runs, which is why the stash-pop after the successful cut also conflicted. They affect nothing a release ships, but under the delegated daily cadence the refusal means most days stall with nobody standing there to stash.

Fix shape, the operator preferring the second: the cleanliness check ignores the tracker's derived exports, or the cut commits them first as their own housekeeping commit so the tag still names a fully-clean tree. The housekeeping commit is stronger - it keeps the archives-match-commit property literal rather than excepted; the builder confirms or argues. Everything else about the refusal was the gate working: it stopped before writing anything and named its reason - preserve that.

Done means a cut on a tree dirty only in the tracker's derived exports proceeds - exports committed as housekeeping, tag naming a clean tree - a tree dirty in anything else still refuses by name, and the stash-pop conflict cannot recur because nothing is stashed.

Review summary: The change does what the work item asked and does it in the shape the operator preferred: the cleanliness gate excludes the two tracker exports via `:(exclude)` pathspecs while still naming any other dirt by file, the exports are committed as their own housekeeping commit placed after the last gate and before the tag so the tag names a tree with nothing uncommitted, the index is put back if that commit fails, and the publishing line becomes `git push --atomic origin <branch> <tag>` only on a day the commit was made. The shell suite genuinely exercises all three acceptance criteria — dirty-only-in-exports proceeds, dirty-in-anything-else refuses by name and leaves no tag, and nothing is stashed — plus the two cases the item did not mention but that decide whether the fix holds: the walkthrough dirtying the exports on its own way through, and the tracker's post-commit export hook, with a self-check proving that fixture's hook actually fires. README.md and docs/developing-yoyo.md are both brought in line with the new behavior, and wiring the suite into `make test` from Go is a reasonable way to make that evidence run in the ordinary loop. One thing blocks approval: the script's own stated prerequisite line, rewritten by this change, names a git floor its new code exceeds, and the gap silently defeats the hooks-off guarantee the housekeeping commit depends on. Note that only a selected subset of invariants was before me, so this is not a statement that the invariants as a whole are satisfied, and documents this change does not touch were not visible to me.
Finding [major] (scripts/cut-release.sh:29): The header now states "Requires git (1.9 or newer, for the `:(exclude)` pathspec the cleanliness check uses)", but the housekeeping commit this same change adds runs `git -c core.hooksPath=/dev/null commit`, and `core.hooksPath` is only honoured from git 2.9. On git 1.9-2.8 the option is unknown config and is silently ignored: the tracker's post-commit export hook runs, `.beads/*.jsonl` are dirty again immediately after the commit that exists to clean them, and the tag names a dirty tree with nothing downstream detecting it — the exact property the change is built to preserve, lost without a message. The printed `git push --atomic ...` likewise needs git 2.4 on the operator's side. Raise the stated floor to 2.9 and name `core.hooksPath` as the reason alongside `:(exclude)`, or suppress the hook in a way the stated floor actually supports.
Finding [minor] (internal/cli/release_repository_test.go:71): TestTheReleaseVerbHousekeepsTheExportsARunAllows asserts the two lists are strictly equal, and the new docs/developing-yoyo.md row instructs "Add the path to both." The lists coincide today but answer different questions — what a run may tolerate the primary checkout acquiring, versus what a release cut may commit on the operator's behalf — so a path legitimately added to `AllowedPrimaryChanges` alone will fail this check and the documented remedy will push someone to make the cut commit a file it should not. Consider asserting containment in the direction that is actually implied, or stating in the row that a deliberate divergence means changing the check rather than the lists.

title: The architect settles the publish shape for approved artifact writes
description: Carved from yoyodyne-ifd.100's rescope as the gate its publish child cites: the architect's design answer on how a typed artifact write's commit and pull request work - how the commit relates to the primary checkout, given a run refuses to start over uncommitted changes; whether the write publishes through a branch and pull request like a run or commits directly under the harness identity; and how the operator's recorded approval relates to the publication. Argued in the architect's conversation, recorded by the operator into the governed designs. Done means the shape is recorded in an architect-owned design or decision record, and yoyodyne-ifd.100.1 can be implemented against it without inventing anything.
notes:
Created under yoyodyne-ifd.100, decomposing it by the development manager in conversation chat-419cedb4a013b063f477e322a2a60466, after turn 45.

Reason: 100.1 was gated on an answer that existed as no item, so nothing stopped the scheduler pulling it and having a developer invent the shape the reviewer refused; this makes the gate real and marks it for the conversation that owns it.

Goal served: A newcomer can go from the documented install to a working first run on their own repository using the readme alone.
Noted by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 237.

Reason: The architect's pending answer is the closer for a recurring operator friction; the evidence lands on the item that carries the question so the decision weighs the operational cost, not only the governance shape.

Operational evidence for the publish-shape answer, from three developer reports on ifd.100's run, 2026-08-23: a document approved from a conversation is written into the primary checkout and left uncommitted, and gitworktree.ValidateReady refuses to start any run while the primary checkout is dirty - so an operator who writes their goals from chat and then asks for work sees 'primary repository has uncommitted changes: docs/product/v1-goals.md' until they commit by hand. The friction is documented and announced on every write, but it is exactly the gap the unimplemented publish step closes, and it makes the shape question concrete: whether the harness commits, opens a pull request, or leaves the file is not just governance - it decides whether writing a document from chat stalls the work loop. The filed amendment on the publish shape should be decided with this in view.
Architect ruling, 2026-08-31, stated whole: the typed artifact-write's output stops at the operator's working tree. Authorize records approval in frontmatter against the revision produced; publication is the operator's own commit under their own identity; until they commit, the document is an uncommitted change and runs refuse to start over it - and the surface that performed the write says so at the moment of writing. Added reason: no path into the target branch exists except a reviewed promotion or the operator's hand - a harness-made commit would be a promotion by another name sweeping in unapproved tree state - and the working-tree stop keeps the artifact read model two-valued: committed state, or operator-pending edit visibly blocking runs. No committed-but-never-operator-touched third state.
close_reason: The architect settled the shape: identical to her conversation-documents rulings, stated whole on this item; 100.1 builds against it.

title: A subagent's result is not the run's terminal result
description:
Run run-841f5ee1866addb533c02a30e67f001a for yoyodyne-ifd.60 died on the second-terminal-result guard while its developer was mid-sentence resolving the last review findings. The developer had spawned Claude Code subagents (system task_started/task_notification events precede it), and a subagent's completion arrives in the parent stream as another type:result envelope -- event 1185 in the recorded stream: empty result text, empty terminal_reason, is_error false -- which the guard from the earlier parser fix reads as a forbidden second terminal result.

The guard was built when no harness developer used subagents; the first one that did lost its run at the finish line, after two repair attempts, with the third attempt's work complete in the worktree.

P0 because subagent use is the model's choice, not the bead's: any run can hit this at any time.
design: Distinguish the run's terminal result from a nested one by shape rather than order: the recorded fixture shows the subagent envelope carries no terminal_reason and no result text, while every genuine terminal carries terminal_reason and usage. Treat a result envelope without those marks as stream noise to record, not a terminal to act on -- same philosophy as the trailing-events fix: guard the invariant (one acted-on terminal), not the surface (one envelope of a type). Replay the exact recorded stream as the regression test. Note the shape on ifd.32 as more provider dialect: nested agent results are something the plugin contract must name.

title: Rewrite the README opening: problem first, and call it yoyo
description:
Operator decision, 2026-08-18, after reviewing candidate openings: direction B, problem-first. The approved opening, verbatim, is the constraint:

'Writing code was never the hard part. Deciding what to build, keeping every change traceable to why, and making sure something other than the author reviewed it before it landed -- that is the work still done by hand around every coding agent. Yoyo is that structure, built to run without you driving each turn: goals in, merged software out, a conversation to steer it.'

And the product is referred to as yoyo in the README's prose, matching the command people actually type. The current opening's defect, named by the operator: 'turns a conversation into merged code' swaps the input for the interface -- it turns goals into code, and the conversation is how the user interacts with those goals.
design:
Structure after the opening: the why-paragraph draws on the brief's own reasoning; the gates become three short bullets (nothing merges unreviewed; the reviewer runs toolless and cannot be talked into a merge; the written goals are the only authority work traces to); the conversation is presented as how you drive it rather than what it is; quick start; the existing honest-bounds section survives as is.

Naming discipline: yoyo in prose; the module path, repository name, and formal references stay Yoyodyne. The naming is settled by the operator, 2026-08-18: the product is called yoyo everywhere in prose because it reads better; yoyodyne remains the project name -- repository, module path, releases, and formal references. No question remains to raise; the brief's prose adopts the same rule in a separate operator-directed change, not in this item, because the brief is not this item's to edit. Every claim must still be true of the current build; the never-ahead-of-reality rule from the last rewrite stands.
acceptance_criteria: The README opens with the approved problem-first text; the product is yoyo in prose with formal names untouched; the gates read as three bullets; the bounds section survives; nothing contradicts the brief, the goals, or the configuration guide; the naming rule -- product yoyo, project yoyodyne -- is applied consistently in the README.

title: Give the backlog owner a live survey, and say when a tracker action touches a closed item
description:
The product manager ordered the backlog from a stale picture. Turn 19 of the 2026-08-18 conversation moved yoyodyne-ifd.23 down-tier citing yoyodyne-ifd.41 as in progress -- both had been closed for hours. Its per-item reads are live, but the open-items survey it reasons from is the one gathered when the conversation opened, external changes never reach a running conversation, and the role that owns backlog ordering is exactly the role that cannot afford a stale list. The harness also applied the priority change to the closed item without a word.

Two fixes. First, a survey tracker action, so the product manager can ask for the current open list mid-conversation the way it already reads single items -- ordering decisions then start from a fresh list as a matter of discipline stated in the persona. Second, act-time honesty: a tracker action whose target's status changed since the conversation's picture of it -- above all one targeting a closed item -- is applied only if still meaningful and its result says plainly what the target's current status is, so reasoning built on a stale premise is corrected at the moment it acts rather than never.
acceptance_criteria: The product manager can request a current backlog survey mid-conversation as a tracker action; the persona directs ordering decisions to start from one; a tracker action on a closed or changed item reports the item's current status in its applied summary; a priority change on a closed item is either refused or applied with the closure stated, never silent; a test replays the ifd.23 case and the reply visibly learns the item is closed.

title: Give product and design artifacts stable identity and metadata
description:
Product and design artifacts have no stable identity. docs/product/brief.md, the goals, the non-goals, docs/designs/, and docs/decisions/ are ordinary Markdown; nothing can reference one durably, so no relationship between them can be validated. Define the identity and metadata schema those artifacts carry: a stable id, an artifact kind, a lifecycle status, and the references the artifact makes upstream.

CONSTRAINT: follow the model yoyodyne-ifd.17 already shipped for invariants rather than inventing a second scheme - the filename is the id, a frontmatter id that disagrees is refused, status is explicit, and changes append to a revision log. Two identity schemes in one repository is the failure to design against. Do not reword any document's prose; this adds identity to what exists. The brief and goals are the product manager's and the operator writes them, so a change to their content is out of scope here even where the metadata sits in the same file.

DONE: an artifact in docs/product, docs/designs, or docs/decisions carries a stable id and metadata validated on load; a malformed or duplicate id is refused with a message naming the file; docs/configuration.md documents the schema.

DECOMPOSITION NOTE: created by the product manager under operator authorization 2026-08-17, because no development manager exists yet - the role arrives with yoyodyne-ifd.4, which yoyodyne-ifd.1 gates. Decomposition belongs to the development manager; this shape should be re-derived or ratified when the role runs.
notes:
Shape check the product manager's warning asked for, done 2026-08-17 by the operator's agent, which can read the design document: the nine children were compared against Milestone 2 verbatim. All seven enumerated capabilities map to a child (IDs 1.1, relationship validation 1.2, role ownership 1.4, change proposals 1.5, staleness 1.6, directive reconciliation 1.7, approvals 1.8), seeding maps to 1.9, and 1.3 is a justified addition from the backlog audit. Two nuances, not gaps: 1.8 covers the durable approval record because the configurable half of approvals already shipped; and Milestone 2 seeds 'brief, goals, and designs' while 1.9 names product and decision artifacts -- the designs home does not exist yet, so whoever builds 1.9 should either create docs/designs/ under the settled ownership or state why seeding defers it.

title: Fix the worktree test that fails its own cleanup
description:
TestManagerIntegrateRefusesNonFastForwardAndKeepsHarnessCommit fails intermittently in CI during teardown, not assertion: 'TempDir RemoveAll cleanup: unlinkat .../repository/.git: directory not empty'. Its checks pass; Go's t.TempDir cleanup then races something still holding or repopulating the repository directory, most likely a git worktree registration or a background git process that has not exited.

Observed on pull request 13 (run 31992104553) for yoyodyne-ifd.21, where it blocked the merge. The same commit passed the harness's own make test, make race and make vet, so this reproduces in CI and not locally.

P0 because build is a required status check on a protected main: a test that fails intermittently in teardown blocks every publication, and the harness cannot merge past it. It also teaches the wrong lesson -- a red required check that is usually spurious is one people stop reading.
design:
Make the test responsible for what it created rather than leaving it to TempDir. A worktree the test registered should be removed by the test before cleanup runs, and any git invocation it started should be waited for, so the directory is genuinely idle when Go tries to delete it.

Prefer fixing the leak to retrying the deletion. A cleanup that retries until the directory goes quiet hides whichever handle is still open, and that handle is the interesting thing: if a git process outlives the call that started it, the harness has the same problem outside tests.

Check the sibling tests in internal/gitworktree for the same shape before assuming this one is unique. The failure is timing-dependent, so the one that fails is not necessarily the only one that can.
acceptance_criteria: The test cleans up the worktrees and processes it creates so TempDir removal has nothing to race; it passes repeatedly under CI conditions, including with -count high enough to expose the race; no cleanup step retries deletion to paper over a held handle; sibling tests with the same pattern are corrected too.
notes:
Found 2026-08-16 when it blocked pull request 13 and stalled the queue. Rerunning the job cleared it, which is the symptom of a flake rather than a fix.

title: Queue the merge with --auto so required checks are waited for
description:
Publishing merges the moment the reviewer approves, but a protected branch will not accept a merge until its required checks have passed. CI takes about forty seconds and the harness asks within seconds of approving, so the merge is refused on essentially every run.

Observed on the first published run, run-ab96b7a966d3b718dc9287d9f5846725 for yoyodyne-ifd.20.1. The run succeeded, the reviewer approved, the work integrated locally and pull request 5 opened, and the merge was refused: 'the base branch's protection rules are not satisfied (BLOCKED) ... the base branch policy prohibits the merge.' GitHub's own message names the remedy: add --auto to have the pull request merged once the requirements are met.

Nothing is lost when this happens -- the outcome is reported as 'the change is integrated locally; the pull request still needs to be reconciled by hand' -- but it leaves an open pull request and an unpushed local branch after every run, which is precisely the manual reconciliation that publishing exists to remove.
design:
Ask GitHub to merge when the requirements are met rather than asking it to merge now. gh pr merge --auto queues the merge and lets the forge complete it once required checks pass, which is what a protected branch is asking for.

Auto-merge is a repository setting, so it can be unavailable. Detect that and say so plainly rather than failing obscurely: a repository with auto-merge disabled and required checks configured cannot be published to this way, and the operator should be told which setting to change.

Do not reach for --admin. Merging with administrator privileges bypasses the very checks the protection expresses, and a harness that routinely overrides branch protection has removed the gate rather than satisfied it.

The confirmation loop needs rethinking alongside this. It currently asks three times over seven seconds whether the merge landed, which suited an immediate merge and cannot suit a queued one. A queued merge completes minutes later, so the run should record the pull request as queued and finish, rather than waiting for something that will not happen while it watches. What reconciliation does about a queued merge that later fails is the open question worth answering here.
acceptance_criteria: A merge into a protected branch with required checks succeeds without manual reconciliation; the harness queues the merge rather than demanding it immediately; a repository that cannot auto-merge is reported with the setting that needs changing rather than a generic refusal; administrator override is never used to bypass protection; a run whose merge is queued finishes and reports the pull request as queued rather than blocking on a confirmation that cannot arrive; reconciliation defines what happens to a queued merge that later fails.
notes:
Found 2026-08-16 on the first run after enabling branch protection and approvals.publishing. P0 because it affects every published run and reintroduces the manual step publishing was meant to remove.

title: Do not discard a completed run over provider output after the terminal result
description:
internal/backend/claudecode/parser.go rejects any line arriving after the provider's terminal result envelope: ParseLine returns 'provider event received after terminal result' as a fatal error. The Claude Code CLI does emit trailing events after its result, so a run whose developer finished successfully is thrown away.

Observed on run-44a559a57d3710e6cd99125efd29ee2d for yoyodyne-ifd.12. The developer completed and emitted its final summary at sequence 586; the run then failed with that parse error, discarding 975 insertions of finished work that never reached checks or review. The error repeated three times in the output, so more than one trailing event arrived.

This is a reliability defect affecting every run, not a problem specific to that work item, which is why it is P0: any run can complete its work and then be discarded for output the provider legitimately emits. It also interacts with yoyodyne-ifd.12, since a rate-limit notice is one of the things plausibly arriving late.
design:
A terminal result means the run's outcome is decided; it does not mean the provider stops writing. Record events that arrive after it rather than failing on them, and keep the already-decided result. Guard the actual invariant, which is that a second terminal result must not silently replace the first, rather than treating all trailing output as corruption.

Preserve what the trailing events carry instead of discarding it. They are exactly where a late rate-limit notice would appear, and yoyodyne-ifd.12 needs that payload. Do not let a post-terminal event mutate the recorded result, session identifier, resolved model, usage, or cost, since those belong to the terminal envelope; append them to the event stream so they remain diagnosable.
acceptance_criteria: A provider event arriving after the terminal result no longer fails the run; the terminal result, session identifier, resolved model, usage, and cost are unchanged by anything arriving after it; trailing events appear in the recorded event stream; a second terminal result is still rejected rather than replacing the first; a test replays a stream with events after the result and asserts the run succeeds with the original outcome intact.

Found 2026-08-16 when ifd.12 was discarded after its developer had already finished. The work is preserved unreviewed at branch yoyodyne/yoyodyne-ifd-12/44a559a5, commit e4ba361, for reference only.
Yoyodyne run passed checks, was approved by an independent reviewer, and was integrated automatically.

title: A registered run.complete action: workflow definitions can express finishing the work
description: From the developer on run-010dd3ae (yoyodyne-ifd.209.5): the delivery action registry has no door onto (*activeRun).finish - recording the outcome on the work item, closing it, and pricing it - so a workflow definition cannot express the completing step at all, and a definition-driven run would promote a change and never close its item. The coverage test in internal/orchestrator/actions_test.go does not catch this because candidate.integrate claims the completing phase. Done means a registered run.complete action exists and the delivery definition uses it, a definition-driven run closes and prices its item exactly as the hard-coded loop does, and the coverage test is held against the steps a run performs rather than only the phases it occupies, so the next missing step fails the test instead of the soak. This blocks the opt-in parity soak (yoyodyne-ifd.209.6) from running the loop end to end.

title: A refused tracker block is recorded, carried, and shown back to the role that sent it
description:
Operator direction (Mason, 2026-09-01): we shouldn't silently drop anything. The refused-whole semantics of tracker blocks is right and STAYS - what changes is the silence around it. Two gaps, one item:

(1) A refused tracker block becomes a durable recorded event - role, action count, refusal reason - so status and the Slack tier can carry it; today it reaches only the invoking terminal, and an automatic wakeup turn's refusal would reach nobody at all.

(2) The refusing role is shown its own refusal at the start of its next turn, verbatim, so it re-issues the lost actions itself instead of believing they landed - today it learns only if a human tells it.

Proof case, named: on 2026-09-01 the product manager's 12-action block was refused whole (limit 10) and the miss was caught only by the operator's assistant checking the tracker afterward - three admissions and seven report dispositions silently gone until re-issued by hand.

Done means a refused block produces a durable event visible in status history, the role's next turn opens with the verbatim refusal, an automatic wakeup's refusal reaches the same surfaces a human-invoked one does, and the proof case replayed self-corrects on the next turn with no human courier.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 359.

Reason: The silence-must-find-you principle applied to the roles' own action path: a governed action channel whose failures evaporate teaches roles to believe in work that never landed - and the proof case was this role's own hand. Freeze-aligned reliability; the wakeup-turn case makes it live before automation deepens.

title: A stall watchdog notices that nothing is happening and says so unprompted
description:
Operator-identified observability gap (Mason, 2026-09-01): nothing detects scheduler silence itself. Today's 7.5-hour dead window (06:05-13:35, the watch dead on the since-fixed transient-read crash) was discoverable only by a human noticing - every existing surface answers when asked, and the DM tier fires on recorded stopped-states, but a dead or wedged scheduler records no state at all, which is why this class keeps costing the most calendar time.

Shape, the operator's: when the tracker reports startable developer work and no run has started for a threshold window, that becomes a durable recorded event - surviving into status history - and the Slack direct-message tier carries it to the operator once per stall, never per check. The checker is the maintenance job or the harness's own loop, builder's choice; the recorded-event-then-DM path is the same one the drift notices (241) and stopped-state DMs already use.

Complements, not duplicates: 51's throughput view and 187's named refusals explain what happened when asked; this notices that nothing is happening and says so unprompted. The operator's framing rides the item: the first two bottleneck classes were bugs since fixed - this is the instrument that catches the next class before it costs half a day.

Done means today's window replayed produces a durable stall event within the threshold and exactly one DM, a clearing stall closes its event, per-check re-firing is impossible by the dedup record, and the event shows in status history afterward.
notes:

Reason: The silence-must-find-you principle applied to its last uncovered case - the process whose death silences everything else. Freeze-aligned reliability at the frontier; delivery is a checker plus one event kind through existing machinery.

title: The idle line says what was passed over and names the conversation that moves next
description:
Operator-admitted status defect, 2026-09-01, three times misleading: when the watch is idle on one slot because the only tracker-ready items are conversation-executor items, the standing line says 'nothing among the N ready item(s) is startable that this session has not already tried. Next: the product manager's - nothing is chosen until work that is ready is admitted.' Both halves mislead: (1) it renders while a developer run is in flight on the other slot, so 'nothing is chosen' reads as a stall while the chain is moving; (2) 'Next: the product manager's' points at admission when the real next mover is the conversation the ready items name - today the architect's, for 212, 203, and 162.

The fix, per the certainty contract (139): the line says what the session actually found - how many ready items were passed over and their why-class (conversation-executed, parked) - and names the conversation that is the true next mover; a refusal names its reason, and the named next actor must be the one who can actually act. The in-flight slot renders on the Running line so idle-on-one-slot never reads as system-idle.

Done means today's state replayed renders 'one run in flight; N ready items passed over: conversation-executed (architect: 212, 203, 162)' in substance, the admission-pointer appears only when admission is genuinely the next act, and the three-times-misleading line is unreproducible.

title: The watch session redeploys itself between runs
description:
Operator feedback (Mason, 2026-08-31): the stale-watch-session problem is still biting - the status warning fired again today with the session 43 harness changes old, and the line says the next move is the operator's; he thought this was fixed. The durable fix: the session redeploys itself.

Why external supervision cannot work, the operator's analysis: the interim maintenance job bounces the watch only when no run is live, because killing the watch cancels its live run - that cancellation has actually happened. With two slots and a deep backlog the scheduler starts the next run the moment one settles, so a 10-minute-cadence external job never lands in an idle window and the session stays stale indefinitely. External supervision at any polling cadence loses this race by construction; only the session itself stands in the gap between runs.

Shape, the development manager's to design: between runs - after a run settles, before the next is claimed - the watch session notices bin/yoyo is newer than its own start and re-executes itself, or exits with a distinct code its supervisor restarts it on. It must never interrupt a live run. The binary-age warning (189's line) then becomes a transient rather than a standing operator chore.

Sequencing note, per the operator: this overlaps the supervision/coordination direction (142) - if the coordination design already absorbs session redeployment, say so here and sequence it there rather than duplicating; the DM checks 142's design before building standalone.

Done means a fix landing on main reaches the resident inside one settle-claim gap with no live run interrupted, the 43-changes-stale case cannot recur as a standing state, and 189's warning is observed transient in practice.

title: Authority inventory: every role-authority check in the harness, enumerated and pinned
description: First authority-workstream child of 209, parallel-safe with the early runtime wave. Enumerate every place the harness enforces role authority in code - tracker action authorization, artifact-write refusal, reviewer topology, promotion and lease guards, protected-path enforcement, conversation-role contracts - as a reviewable artifact, with a repository test pinning the enumeration to the code so a new authority check cannot appear unlisted. The inventory is the ground truth the capability registry re-expresses, so its completeness is the workstream's safety, exactly as 211's baseline is the runtime's. Done means: the enumeration exists as a reviewable document naming each check's location, the role it binds, and what it refuses; the pinning test fails if a listed check moves or an authorization site appears outside the list; no behavior changes; the diff is shown whole to review. Dispatch waits on the hardening freeze per the epic's note.

title: Every run and resident pins the harness build it ran, and the records prove deployment
description:
From four reports across 195 and 201, 2026-08-31, the week's largest retrospective finding: the resident scheduler ran a stale binary through the storm. The four substituted repair dispatches (180, 182 on 08-27; 143, 68.22 on 08-30) all happened AFTER 178's refusal merged on 08-27 09:47, and the refusal is test-proven on the dispatch path - so the dispatching process cannot have run main. The phantom invariant warning ran six days (24 runs) from a binary predating its own in-tree fix, stopping only when bin/yoyo was rebuilt 08-30 20:54. watch.jsonl began stamping builds only 08-30 11:15, so the records cannot say which binary did what before then. Most of the week's 'code defects' were deployment defects, undiagnosable as such.

Scope: every run record pins the harness build (commit or digest) alongside backend, model, account alias, and configuration revision - the durable-state invariant's missing field; every resident stamps its build in its own records from process start; and the staleness heartbeat (189, landed) reads these rather than inferring. Done means a substituted-dispatch or phantom-warning incident is answerable from records alone - which build did this - and a fix landing on main while a stale resident runs is visible as the named degraded state 189 defines, with the build gap stated.

description:

His goal: get as much of the hard-coded logic into configuration files as possible, starting with the workflow graph. The brief's spine: replace hard-coded workflow topology with versioned declarative state-machine definitions, preserving current behavior first; configuration chooses sequence but cannot grant capability - actions, role authority, Git operations, evidence validation, and leases stay in trusted Go; every instance pinned to its definition digest; in-flight work never silently migrated.

SEQUENCE, recorded for the DM's decomposition under this epic once the architect's design lands: (1) behavioral baseline golden tests - the enabling first step, admitted alongside; (2) the architect's promotion of the full brief - precedes implementation; (3) the brief's runtime sequence in its own order: schemas and capability/action registries wrapping existing code, strict loaders and compiler, checkpointed execution, the delivery loop encoded as built-in data, opt-in parity soak with legacy runs resumable, declarative default, project-owned files, then triage and management conversions, agent context, Sentinel, triggers, specialist reuse. The authority workstream interleaves per the brief: inventory, capability registry, default bundles expressing the five roles, capability-based authorization, separation policy - all reaching parity BEFORE configurable role definitions are admitted; that ordering is held as non-negotiable.

title: An operator-decided escalation can clear or raise an item's caps, recorded and attributed
description:
The durable fix from the DM's deadlock ruling, 2026-08-30. The escalation protocol currently ends in decisions nobody can execute: the rounds-cap check refuses the DM's rerun recording regardless of the operator's decision (refused at 5-of-4 and 6-of-4 on the two priority items), the rerun verbs refuse without that ledger record, and the escalation entry satisfies neither - so a cap-exhausted item is permanently unrunnable by any recorded path, and the operator's REBUILD decisions had to be executed by admitting fresh items instead.

Scope: an operator-decided escalation outcome can clear or raise an item's rounds cap through a recorded, attributed override - the ledger accepts it as an operator decision, the verbs honor it, and the override names who decided and when. The caps' purpose is preserved: they stop machines looping, and only an operator's recorded decision crosses them - no agent path, no default. Done means the 143/68.22 deadlock replayed resolves through the recorded override rather than through fresh-item surgery, and the escalation protocol's decisions are executable end to end.

title: An empty-diff round is an environmental refusal: it spends no budget and counts toward no cap
description:
Operator admission, 2026-08-30, extending 187's own definition: an empty-diff round is an environmental refusal - the run delivered nothing because the environment handed it nothing - so it must not spend the item's repair budget or count toward its rounds cap. Tonight it did, three times: the doorbell tests, pooling, and the environmental-refusal item itself each burned a granted round on a clean worktree the stale-binary dispatch handed them.

Scope: a round whose diff is empty and whose run records an environmental cause - handback-missing-change, dirty primary, sandbox spawn failure, stale-binary dispatch - is classified environmental at settle: budget unspent, cap untouched, the cause named in the round's record, and the item stays where it was rather than advancing toward escalation. A genuinely empty delivery with no environmental cause recorded still spends, so laziness cannot hide in the class - which composes with the review pipeline carrying the developer's outcome report (148), the evidence that distinguishes the two.

description:

Scope: the heartbeat carries the resident's binary age - 'this session runs a build from before N harness changes landed; restart to deploy them' - and crossing a threshold joins the operator-DM tier as a system-degraded state, said once per the tier's discipline. This is interim visibility until the supervision design's restart ownership (130.1's service-plus-thin-client target) retires the class structurally: a supervised resident restarts on deploy, and this heartbeat line is the bridge until then.

Done means a resident running a pre-fix binary says so in every heartbeat with the count, the threshold crossing DMs the operators once, and tonight's case replayed announces itself before the first granted round is spent against a dead bug.

title: Parked work is unschedulable: a status the scheduler respects, not a priority it drains to
description:
From Thursday's tail, 2026-08-27: the scheduler drained the queue to priority 4 and ran the PARKED Codex adapter - ifd.6, $34.38, failed - because parked-by-priority is schedulable whenever the queue empties, contradicting the scope decision's off-the-critical-path intent. The product manager's own convention created the gap: priority 4 as parking is a reading the scheduler does not share, and watch mode makes queue-draining routine, so every parked item is one thin day from being paid for.

Scope, the operator's two options, builder decides with reasoning: a parked status the scheduler respects - never selected regardless of queue depth, visibly distinct in listings - or a deliberate floor above 4 that selection never crosses without an explicit operator release. Either way, done means the current parked set (the Codex adapter, the plugin contract, contributor mode, fork publishing, external config) cannot be selected by a drained queue, the parking is visible as parking rather than as low priority, and the ifd.6 case replayed selects nothing.

title: An environmental refusal is a named state the operator hears about, never a tried-memory entry
description:
Operator ask after the third silent-stall incident, 2026-08-27, three fixes as one behavior. The incident: a two-line hand edit sat uncommitted in the primary checkout - correct per the architect's conversation-documents ruling, runs refuse a dirty primary - but the refusal was invisible: the watch session marked every ready item already-tried and idled, the heartbeat said nothing-startable without saying WHY, and the operator diagnosed it by asking his assistant, twice, days apart.

(1) A run start refused for a dirty primary checkout is a NAMED state, not a tried-memory entry: the watch retries it each pass, and the heartbeat says exactly 'runs cannot start: uncommitted changes in the primary checkout (<file>); commit or stash to release' - whose-move the operator's. (2) That state joins the DM tier the moment 68.20 lands: it is a system-stopped state by that item's own definition, so the operator's phone says it, once, with the file named. (3) The tried-memory poisoning generalizes: environmental refusals - dirty checkout, capacity, sandbox failure - must NEVER mark an item tried; only the item's own failures may, or every environmental stall reads as an exhausted queue.

Done means the dirty-primary case replays as a retrying named state with the exact heartbeat line, the DM tier carries it once 68.20 lands, no environmental refusal class writes tried-memory, and the three recorded incidents' silence is structurally impossible.

title: Runs prove they can execute at minute zero, and submit to review only with execution evidence
description: The two implementation halves of the operator's 2026-08-23 principle, beside the architect's invariant wording. (1) Sandbox self-check at run start: the developer environment proves it can execute a trivial command before development begins, and a run that cannot is refused loudly at minute zero instead of spending an hour blind - tonight's runs discovered E2BIG at first use, after context was spent. (2) The handoff bar: a developer run submits to review only with evidence it exercised its own change - build and the declared checks it can run - and absent that evidence the run stops rather than submits, so blind never looks routine again. Done means a run in tonight's environment refuses at start naming the spawn failure, a run that built nothing cannot reach review silently, the evidence appears in what the reviewer receives (composing with 148's bundle work), and the 149 case - zero checks, delivered as done - is structurally unrepeatable.

title: A handback carries the preserved change, not a clean worktree

title: A moved remote target cannot close an item as integrated into a state nothing resolves
description:
From the reviewer on ifd.154's verification run, 2026-08-23 - a live defect on the current publishing path, not the hypothetical team-mode one: when the remote target moves under a run (any human push to main during a run suffices), the local promotion has already happened, ErrRemoteTargetDrift cannot fail the run, the work item closes as integrated, and CatchUpTarget then refuses to reconcile the diverged local target because 'only a person can say which history is right'. An outstanding publication is recorded, and nothing resolves it - a permanent wedge the operator discovers later. Routed only as a Work-discovered bullet in docs/diagnoses/yoyodyne-ifd-154-promotion-precondition.md until now.

Scope, per the report's citations: internal/orchestrator/publish.go's recordPublishFailure path and internal/gitworktree/converge.go:113-121. Done means a target moved under a run cannot produce an item recorded integrated against a divergence nothing owns: either the drift fails the run before the item closes, or the outstanding publication routes to an owner (the docket, or reconcile with 170's forge re-ask) with the divergence named - and the human-push-during-run case replays into a resolvable state.

title: The system-stopped states DM the operators: the push half of the heartbeat
description:
Operator request from today's brake, 2026-08-23, for the Slack epic. Direct messages to the operators - plural, from the mapping - when the system as a whole waits on a person: the channel heartbeat worked, he read it and asked, but a channel line is something you find when you look, and the all-stopped state is the one condition that deserves to find YOU.

The noise discipline, his shape: a single blocked item stays a channel warning with its status reaction - it has an owner (the DM docket), and DMing every block would teach operators to ignore DMs. The DM tier is reserved for system-waits-on-human states: the brake tripping (nothing new chosen until a human releases), the capacity-blocked state past its wait budget, and plausibly a directive or escalation naming the operator explicitly. Each DM says what stopped, why, whose move it is, and where the full record lives, tagged per the operators mapping; the brake release cancels its own follow-ups.

Mechanics for the builder: the app manifest likely needs the im:write scope - another workspace-approval click, worth bundling with any other pending scope change so the operator approves once.

Done means the three named states produce DMs to mapped operators with the four contents, a single blocked item produces no DM, release cancels follow-ups, and the scope change ships bundled. Pairs with the heartbeat as the push half of one principle: silence must never mean waiting-on-you-without-telling-you, and a stopped line should not depend on the operator checking the channel.

If anything rewrites a parked run's state while it waits — a supervisor pass, a reconciliation, a retry that re-records the same usage limit — the two-hour budget restarts and this state never escalates, which is silent failure of exactly the condition the tier exists for. title: Each cut writes release notes: key functionality, enhancements, fixes
description:
Operator requirement, 2026-08-23. With each release tagged, a release notes file is produced - what was added since the last tag - organized as key functionality at the top, enhancements below, bug fixes at the bottom, with one exception: a critical bug fix may go up with key functionality. The judgment of key versus enhancement versus fix is the product manager's until the post-v1 release-manager role exists (recorded as post-v1 intent beside the operations role).

Mechanics: the raw material is what landed between the last tag and this one - the closed items with their titles, types, and goals, richer than commit messages; the notes live versioned in the repository (a releases or notes home the cut writes, the file named for the tag it cuts) so the release page and the repository tell one story. Composes with the daily delegation: the release-worthy call produces the tag, the reason in the channel, and the notes file - one act, three outputs.

First exercise and acceptance case: v0.3.0's notes, written retroactively covering v0.2.0 to v0.3.0 - five days of the system building its own scheduler, triage, Slack stack, installer, and security remediation - authored by the product manager's judgment from the generated raw material. Done means the cut produces the notes file from the closed-item material, the sections follow the operator's shape, the v0.3.0 retroactive notes exist in the notes home, and the daily cadence ships notes with every tag thereafter.

title: Dependency links bind in-flight items: run-start and repair re-check what selection checked
description: From four reports on ifd.100.1's run, 2026-08-23, the sharpest from the developer: the DM's dependency link on 100.2 was applied while 100.1 was already in_progress - the link's own applied-summary records it - and the run-start path never re-checked, so the gate filed expressly to stop a developer inventing the unsettled publish shape stopped nothing. title: Verify the promotion precondition the team-mode design leans on
description: Bounded verification commission, the ifd.97 pattern, from the reviewer's warning on ifd.82.2's run, 2026-08-23: the design's cross-machine promotion safety argument rests entirely on an asserted property of the existing promotion path - that before the forge merges, the remote target must already contain the commit the run was written against and carry exactly its content, so a target another machine moved fails closed and replays. title: The architect rules on the release push: a second writer of main and the promotion lease
description: EXECUTOR: conversation:architect. From both reviewer warnings on ifd.150's run, 2026-08-23: scripts/cut-release.sh now advances local main by a housekeeping commit and instructs git push --atomic origin main <tag> - previously the cut only created a tag. That introduces a writer of origin/main that takes no promotion lease, alongside the harness path that one-promotion-per-target-branch serializes. The reviewers' own analysis: it looks safe in practice - a concurrent harness promotion makes the operator's atomic push a rejected non-fast-forward rather than a lost update, and the pre-tag HEAD-vs-origin/main gate catches divergence on the next cut - but under the delegated daily cadence the push becomes routine, a rejected push wedges the next cut until someone reconciles by hand, and nobody has decided who runs the push or what they do on rejection. The architect decides whether an operator-run release script advancing the integration branch belongs inside the invariant's scope, and the who-pushes-and-what-on-rejection procedure is recorded with the ruling. Interim mitigation, recorded: under delegation the product manager triggers cuts, and a rejected push means the cut waits with the reason in the channel rather than a hand-reconciliation under time pressure.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 214.

Reason: The publishing goal's invariant - one serialized writer of the target - now has an undecided second writer arriving with tomorrow's cadence; the ruling belongs to the architect and should exist before rejected pushes become a routine operational state. Conversation-executed, marked so per the 144 practice.

Goal served: Publish that work as pull requests the harness opens, and has the forge merge, on the roles' behalf, for projects that enable it, without letting any agent push or merge.
Noted by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 224.

Reason: Both reports land on the item the architect already holds; the race window and the destructive-recovery fact are exactly what the ruling must answer, recorded where she reads it.

Two sharpenings for the architect's ruling, from reviewer and developer warnings on ifd.150's later run, 2026-08-23. (1) The race window is precise now: a harness promotion arriving between the HEAD-equals-origin/main gate and the housekeeping commit leaves the tag naming a tree the archives were not built from - a read-then-move on the serialized branch performed by an operator verb with no run and no lease. (2) The rejection path is undocumented and its obvious recovery is destructive: nothing in the script, README, or developing-yoyo says what to do when the atomic push is refused, and pull --rebase rewrites the housekeeping commit and orphans the tag - worse than the rejection. The ruling should therefore settle three things: whether the cut takes the promotion lease (or the invariant extends to branch moves outside a run), whether the verb pushes the branch before tagging, and what the documented recovery is when a push is refused anyway.
Architect ruling, 2026-08-31: the release tag push is blessed with bounds, not bound into the lease. A tag push publishes an immutable name for an existing commit and moves no branch - not the read-then-move race the promotion lease prevents. Bounds: the tag names a commit already on the remote target, never forced, never moves a branch, pushed by the operator's own Git under their identity; the harness and agents push no tags; and the boundary is the operation, not the ceremony - any release step that MOVES a branch is a promotion and takes the lease. That last sentence is the line a future release script would otherwise cross without noticing.
close_reason: Ruled: blessed with bounds, recorded on the item.

title: The attribution-destroying writer is guarded and the witness backfill runs
description:
From the ifd.122 diagnosis findings, delivered as two critical reports 2026-08-20 and unhandled since; the full diagnosis is docs/diagnoses/yoyodyne-ifd-122-goal-attribution-loss.md. The writer that destroyed 12 goal attributions is still live and still silent: bd update with --notes replaces notes wholesale, agent sessions use it routinely - twice within minutes of the fix shipping - and nothing warns against it in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md. ifd.108's witness protects only items attributed by the post-fix harness, because the yoyo goals witness backfill (internal/cli/goals.go:192) has never been run - so a loss on the majority of items still reports as the one grandfathered state that never fails.

Scope, per the diagnosis: run the witness backfill so every attributed item is protected, not only post-fix ones; make wholesale notes replacement unable to silently destroy an attribution - guarded, refused, or attribution-preserving, the builder decides which with reasoning; and the agent instruction files warn against the wholesale writer. Done means the backfill has run and is verified, no routine agent path can silently erase an attribution, and the instructions say so.

title: The reviewer's evidence matches what its judgments require
description:
Consolidates four critical reports, 2026-08-20 through 2026-08-23, one defect: the reviewer judges with less evidence than its findings claim. (1) On 100.1 the reviewer could not see the blocking dependency the item is correctly refused on, and issued blocker findings instructing the developer to implement a design the architect has not decided - repair pressure toward an unauthorized design, the exact outcome the dependency link exists to prevent. (2) On 68.9 it twice asserted a repository file does not exist because no binary appears in the diff (the blob is in HEAD and main), and miscounted literal file content, directing an edit that would have introduced the defect the item fixes. (3) On 121.3, three consecutive reviews lacked the developer's change summary while the item's done criterion names that summary as evidence, and lacked README.md while the criterion requires verbatim comparison against it - both repair attempts consumed on missing evidence.

Scope: the reviewer's bundle includes the item's dependency state (blocked-on and why); file access at HEAD for existence and content claims, not diff-only inference; the developer's change summary; and sources the acceptance criteria cite. And one loop-shape change: a developer's reasoned refusal to implement - blocked on an undecided upstream - is a terminal outcome review can accept, not a finding to repair. Done means each of the three cases replayed reviews correctly, and no finding can assert a file's absence without the bundle having been able to check.

title: Conversation-executed items carry an executor marker the scheduler respects
description:
Development manager's admission request from tonight's role-routing stoppage, 2026-08-22. Work items whose executor is a persona conversation rather than a developer run have no marker selection respects: the architect's brief-promotion item (138) was selected as an ordinary developer item and burned a full run plus two review rounds producing a correctly-refused empty diff. Her subtler cost: those rounds count against the item's rounds cap, so a twice-mis-selected conversation item reaches its cap having done nothing and forces a spurious escalation.

Fix shape, hers: an executor field or equivalent marker at admission, respected by selection - the protected-path gate already proves such items are not developer-writable, so selection is the cheapest place to stop the mismatch. Done means an item admitted as conversation-executed is never selected for a developer run, the marker is set at admission and visible in the queue, existing conversation-class items (the brief promotion, the team-mode scoping, design items) are marked, and a mis-selection replay of the 138 case selects nothing and says why.

Admission-side half, owned by the product manager: items whose execution is a persona conversation get the marker at admission from now on - the 138 exposure existed because its conversational executor lived in prose only.

title: The sink paces catch-up and digests deep backlogs instead of flooding into suppression
description:
Companion to yoyodyne-ifd.68.7, from the same 2026-08-20 restart: the catch-up flood was rate-limited by Slack ('due to a high volume of activity, we are not displaying some messages sent by this application'), and Slack's suppression hides messages permanently rather than delaying them - an unpaced catch-up converts the design's arrive-late-never-dropped promise into dropped-from-view for the overflow. Twelve hours of cursors replayed at full speed will do this on every long-gap restart.

The fix: the sink paces posts to Slack's sustained tolerance (about one per second per channel); honors 429 Retry-After when the API says so; and gains a digest mode for deep backlogs - full fidelity for the recent window, one summarizing message per thread for older accumulation ('this item accumulated N events while reporting was down; the record holds them'), which serves Slack's limits and the reader equally, since nobody scrolls four hundred replayed messages.

Done means a long-gap restart replays without triggering suppression, 429s are honored, deep backlogs digest per thread with the durable record named as the full account, and the recent window keeps full fidelity. Same builder should take this and 68.7 together: one restart, two halves of surviving it.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 137.

Reason: Suppression hides messages and a four-hundred-message replay hides the signal; both fail the reader the channel exists for, and the digest is the legibility goal's important-findings-stand-out clause applied to catch-up. Priority 2 beside 68.7, its pair from the same outage, per the operator.

Goal served: The harness's surfaces read clearly: boundaries between topics and speakers are visible, important findings stand out, and every distinction survives a terminal that cannot render emphasis.

title: The Slack sink tolerates additive schema changes instead of starving on them
description:
From the operator's overnight sink outage, 2026-08-20. ifd.118 added work_item_title to run records; the long-running sink - an older binary by hours - decodes run state with unknown fields refused, so every pass failed on the first new-format record and retried forever with cursors unchanged. It reported loudly and lost nothing, but the remedy was never named, and the collision is structural under watch mode: schema-touching changes land while the sink runs, every time.

The fix: the sink tolerates unknown fields when reading records - it is a reader of other processes' output, and additive fields are the compatible evolution the envelope's schema_version exists for. Where a record is genuinely undecodable, it skips it with a stated skip and tells the operator plainly that the running sink is older than the records and a restart is the remedy.

Same lesson as the verdict-drift failure that cost a run (the severity_note unknown field, recorded on ifd.32's provider evidence): strict decoding of another process's evolving output is an outage generator. Done means an older sink survives additive fields silently, an undecodable record is skipped with the skip stated and the restart remedy named, and the ifd.118 deploy replayed against a running older sink loses no thread and no cursor progress.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 135.

Reason: The Slack channel is the visibility that makes unattended operation acceptable, and a sink that starves whenever a deploy outpaces it takes that visibility down on exactly the nights watch mode runs unwatched. title: An unresolvable reference in item text is omitted with a stated omission, never a pre-flight failure
description:
Sibling of ifd.116, from live triage 2026-08-20. Context validation fails a run when an item's notes contain a reference that is not repository-relative: ifd.121's repair cannot start because its triage notes quote the reviewer's citation 'a parent-relative README path (the literal token is defused here because quoting it wedged this very item — the recursion is the bug's best evidence)', and notes are append-only by directive, so the item is permanently wedged - the same shape as ifd.25's oversized-reference wedge that ifd.116 fixed.

The rule, ifd.116's principle extended: a reference that cannot be resolved - malformed, relative, pointing nowhere - is omitted from the assembled context with a stated omission the developer reads, never a pre-flight failure. Review text quotes paths in every verdict; every quoted path is otherwise a future landmine in an append-only field.

Done means an item whose notes carry unresolvable references runs, the omission is stated in the context where the developer sees it, resolvable references still resolve, and the ifd.121 case replayed starts its repair. Priority 1: it blocks the DM-ordered README repair today and recurs structurally with every quoted relative path.

Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 132.

Reason: A run that no human can unwedge because the wedging text is append-only defeats unattended operation structurally, and the trigger - a reviewer quoting a path - is produced by the loop itself every cycle. title: Scheduler selection guard: an epic with open execution children is not itself runnable
description:
From the development manager's overnight triage, 2026-08-20. The scheduler pulled yoyodyne-ifd.121 and yoyodyne-ifd.121.2 as two parallel wholesale README rewrites: double spend, a guaranteed integration conflict for the second to land, and the three-block failure storm that tripped the brake. An epic whose open children cover its execution must not itself be selected as developer work.

Two candidate fixes, the builder decides which, the guard being the smaller: a selection guard - the scheduler skips an item whose open children cover its execution - or decomposition stripping an epic of runnable scope when its execution child is created. Either way, done means an epic with open execution children is never pulled as a run while those children exist, the skip records its reason like any selection decision, and the ifd.121 case replayed selects only the child.

Priority 1 case, per the DM: watch mode makes selection continuous, so this repeats on every epic-plus-child pair in the ready queue until fixed.
notes:
Admitted to the backlog by the product manager in conversation chat-91253e0e070c17b0663651cc48602122, after turn 130.

Reason: Unattended selection choosing a container and its child as duplicate work makes continuous autonomy wasteful and conflict-generating by construction; the guard is what keeps the loop's choosing sound now that nothing waits for a human between pulls. Admitted directly under goal-level admission from the DM's triage warning, which the operator relayed.

title: A proposal approved in --message chat never becomes an item: the y decision does not complete
description: The PM's critical of 2026-08-20, filed via direct bd write because this bug plus the work_items gate had wedged every other admission path (the emergency use the retiring practice exists for): two operator approvals ('y' in yoyo chat --message) of pending proposals produced no admissions — surveys straddling them show an unchanged queue, and the operator's y evidently arrives as ordinary chat text rather than reaching the proposal decision surface, the same seam class as the fixed /reports leak but on the admission path. Interactive-mode approval may work; --message approval demonstrably does not. Done means: an approval token in --message mode decides the pending proposal exactly as interactively, a refused or expired proposal says so rather than silently dropping, the decision (either way) is durable on the conversation record, and a test drives propose-then-approve through the --message path end to end. Also fold in, per the PM's paired warning: configuration support for the operator's recorded diagnosis-class carve-out (read-only, bounded, findings-only items admissible under work_items: human), so the policy stops being dead letter for projects that keep the human gate; and surface the reviewer's flagged contradiction — the design says lower-level gates are configurable but disabled by default, ifd.25 shipped human enabled — to the architect for an amendment or a default change.
